projects.title: ONE MORE SPIN
projects.tagline: Roulette meets roguelike. Made in 6 days for a game jam and now in post-jam development.

facts.role: Programming and game design. We split the work 50/50 and both worked on every part.
facts.context: Game jam (The Very Serious Juniper Dev Game Jam)

cover.alt: ONE MORE SPIN gameplay: roulette table with a +130 payout popping over the wheel

gallery.alt: A winning spin with a +130 payout, quota and round tracker on the right
The ball lands on 34, with chips on red and on single numbers
Between-round shop with relics and chip upgrades bought with coins
Main menu with Play, Options and Quit
ONE MORE SPIN cover art with roulette wheel and casino chips

projects.overview: ONE MORE SPIN turns European roulette into a roguelike. Every round you get a few spins to reach a score quota. You place chips on numbers and outside bets, and between rounds you spend coins in a shop on relics and chip upgrades that change your odds. The jam themes were "Spin to Win" and "Very Serious". We built the jam version in six days as a team of two and kept working on it after the jam.
built: GameManager singleton that keeps track of rounds, spins, quota, coins and progression
Bet system that stores all active bets in a list, so you can place as many chips as you like and each one is resolved on its own
Drag and drop for placing chips on the table
Animated feedback with Tweens, like payout popups and a quota counter that counts up
Shop between rounds with relics and chip upgrades
Options menu with separate music and SFX volume, saved with ConfigFile and reachable from the main menu and the pause menu
projects.challenge: In our first version the UI updated the moment a spin was resolved. The numbers changed before the animations had even played, so the game felt out of sync and sometimes jumped to the next round too early. We fixed this by separating the game state from what is shown on screen. The state updates right away, but the labels only change once a Tween has finished, and the next step (overlay, win sound, next round) is started by a callback at the end of the animation. Spins became much easier to follow and a few round counting bugs disappeared along the way.
projects.differently: Roulette only gives you one number per spin, so there aren't many things that can trigger at once. In games like Balatro a good hand sets off a long chain of effects, and that is a big part of why they feel so satisfying. For the post-jam version I'm working on modifiers that each trigger separately, so a strong late-game spin turns into a chain of payouts instead of one big number.

devlog.title: Engine, repo and structure
devlog.text: We picked Godot because its scene files are plain text, which makes working on the same project with Git much easier for two people. Then we set up a GitHub repo, a shared folder structure and an empty GameManager so both of us started from the same base.

devlog.title: GameManager and first playable spin
devlog.text: The GameManager became an autoload with spin(), place_bet() and resolve_bet(). Early on we decided that it only holds data and every UI element updates itself. That kept scene changes simple and the code easy to follow.

devlog.title: Pixel art and layout
devlog.text: We drew our own 32×32 chip sprites, set up pixel-perfect import settings and tried a few layouts until the wheel, the table and the quota panel worked together. We went with European roulette with a single zero.

devlog.title: One script for every field
devlog.text: All fields on the table share one script with an exported bet type, so adding a new bet type is just a setting in the editor. Bets are stored in a list, which lets players spread chips across the table and get each one paid out separately.

devlog.title: Animations, sound and menus
devlog.text: We added Tween animations for payouts and the quota counter, a quota overlay, chip and win sounds, drag and drop chips that stay on top while dragging, and an options and pause menu with saved volume settings.

devlog.title: Two versions on itch.io and a new scoring idea
devlog.text: The jam version and the post-jam version are both available on itch.io. For the post-jam version we're working on modifiers that trigger one after another, so strong spins build up into a chain of payouts.

steps.title: Place chips
steps.text: Every table field has a bet_type. Dropping a chip calls GameManager.place_bet().

steps.title: Store bets
steps.text: Each bet goes into an active_bets list, so any number of chips can be on the table.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.text: Every bet in the list is checked on its own and adds to the score.

steps.title: Animate
steps.text: The UI plays Tweens and only moves on to the overlay or next round when the animation's callback fires.

projects.title: Camping Diorama
projects.tagline: A stylized camping scene I made on my own, from modelling in Blender to rendering in Unreal Engine 5.

facts.role: Everything (modelling, UVs, rigging, texturing, scene setup, lighting, rendering)

cover.alt: Stylized low-poly camping diorama with tent, campfire, chairs, pine trees and a river

gallery.alt: Full diorama rendered in Unreal Engine 5

projects.overview: A small stylized diorama that I built completely on my own. I modelled every asset in Blender, unwrapped and textured them in Substance Painter, added a bone based wind rig and put everything together in Unreal Engine 5, where I also did the lighting and rendered the final showcase video. The tent is the hero asset.
built: Modelled every asset in Blender, with the tent as the hero asset
UV mapping and a stylized low poly texturing workflow in Substance Painter
Bone based wind rigs for the animation
Scripted FBX export from Blender to Unreal Engine
Master material, scene setup and lighting in UE5
Animated camera showcase rendered with the Level Sequencer
projects.challenge: Before this project I had barely used any of the three tools. The hardest part was learning Blender, Substance Painter and Unreal Engine 5 well enough to use them properly, in about 75 hours in total. What helped most was setting up a fixed workflow early on: one stylized texturing approach, a script for the FBX export and a single master material in Unreal. After that every new asset went through the same steps and I didn't have to figure things out from scratch each time.

breakdown.title: Hero asset: the tent
breakdown.text: The tent got the most attention. It has an olive canvas, a beige lower part with a leather edge, painted seam lines and a small plaid patch near one of the rope anchors. Details from a separate high-poly roof were baked onto the low-poly tent in Substance Painter.

images.alt: Textured tent hero asset rendered in UE5
Clay render of the tent showing the pure form
Wireframe of the tent showing the topology

breakdown.title: UV mapping
breakdown.text: I placed seams the way the real object is sewn or built, for example along fabric panels and on the back side of chair legs. A checker texture helped me keep the texel density even, and the tent gets more texture space than small or hidden parts.

breakdown.title: Texturing in Substance Painter
breakdown.text: All assets follow one stylized look with flat colours, light grunge and a bit of edge wear. On the tent I used a position generator for the leather edge at the bottom, a grunge map in multiply mode and hand-painted seams.

breakdown.title: Wind rig
breakdown.text: Every moving asset has its own armature: the tent's curtains and canvas, the trees, cattails, grass blades, the river surface and the chairs. All of them follow the same gust curve, so the wind peaks across the whole scene at the same moment. Grass and river waves use offset phases so the motion doesn't look copied.

breakdown.title: Assembly and lighting in UE5
breakdown.text: The assets came into Unreal as skeletal meshes with looping animations. One master material with packed ORM textures and a material instance per asset kept the setup simple. The lighting is a low afternoon sun, a post process volume with a bit more contrast and saturation, and fixed exposure for the camera flight.

projects.differently: A lot of my time went into learning the tools while I was already building. With what I know now I would plan the project in clear phases with time estimates from the start, set up the workflow first and then work through the assets in a more structured order.

projects.title: Minecraft Fabric Mods
projects.tagline: Two client-side mods for Minecraft challenge runs, published on Modrinth.

facts.duration: 2 days (one to build both mods, one to update them to 26.3)

cover.alt: All Items overview grid showing collected, skipped and remaining items

gallery.alt: Challenge Timer above the hotbar in the default style
Challenge Timer with custom red colour and background
All Items HUD showing the current target item and progress
All Items overview with done, skipped and remaining items

projects.overview: Two small client-side Fabric mods for singleplayer challenge runs, the kind you know from Let's Plays. Challenge Timer puts a run timer above the hotbar. All Items gives you every item in the game one by one in random order, and you have to collect all of them. Both are on Modrinth and work with Minecraft 26.2 and 26.3.
built: Challenge Timer: real time run timer that pauses in the pause menu, grows its format from seconds up to days and is controlled with commands
All Items: the item list is read from the game's registry at runtime instead of being hardcoded, so it always matches the installed version
Potions, tipped arrows and enchanted books are split into one entry per variant
Random order based on a seed, automatic detection in inventory, off-hand and armour slots, and a warning for items you can't get in survival
Scrollable overview of done, skipped and remaining items, sorted alphabetically so the upcoming order stays secret
Custom HUD with adjustable hex colour and background, progress saved per world as JSON
Updated both mods to Minecraft 26.3 and its API changes
projects.challenge: The gameplay code itself was pretty simple. What took more effort was getting from a mod that ran fine in my dev environment to a release that anyone can download and use straight away. That meant packaging it properly, setting the right dependencies and version info, and publishing it on Modrinth so players only have to drop it into their mods folder.

snippets.title: Building the item list at runtime
snippets.note: The mod never ships a fixed item list. It walks the game's item registry when a challenge starts, expands items with variants and shuffles the result with the chosen seed, so the same seed always gives the same order.

projects.title: Campus Balance Run
projects.tagline: Endless runner about student wellbeing, made for Ashoka and the Campus Wellbeing Project. Now played on campuses worldwide.

facts.team: 5 students: Isabella Lehmann, Anika Böhning, Carl Bob, Marcel Sanchez Velez and me
facts.engine: No engine, plain HTML5 and JavaScript
facts.context: University client project for Ashoka and the Campus Wellbeing Project, Game Design course with Prof. Dr. Anna Rebecca Unterholzner

cover.alt: Campus Balance Run title screen with the sprout mascot running across campus

gallery.alt: Title screen with the mascot and the Campus Wellbeing Project logo
Gameplay: running down a corridor with Energy, Social and Balance meters at the top
Results screen showing collected items and distance
Credits screen listing the development team and course

projects.overview: Ashoka and the Campus Wellbeing Project asked our course for a game that supports the project's message. We made an endless runner in the style of Subway Surfers. You run across campus and keep collecting orbs for Energy, Social and Balance. If one of them runs empty, the run is over. The game runs in any browser and is now used at campuses around the world. I wrote all of the game code. My teammates did the visual design, the documentation and a promo video.
built: All of the game code in plain JavaScript without an engine, so it runs in every browser, phones included
Movement between three lanes and the endless forward scrolling
Energy, Social and Balance meters that drain over time and refill when you collect orbs
Spawning of obstacles and pickups, distance tracking and the results screen
Putting the team's art and UI into a portrait layout that works well on phones
projects.challenge: The game had to be very small and run on as many devices as possible, even on a bad internet connection, because it is also played in countries where internet access is limited. I kept the download tiny by handling as much as possible in code: the team's assets are scaled and reused at runtime instead of shipping many large files, so everything still looks right but loads quickly on weak phones and slow networks.
projects.differently: I would set a size budget for every type of asset at the very start and test on old phones and throttled connections from the first week. That way the art could have been produced at the right size from the beginning instead of being reduced later.
